title: Al-Wakil, the Trustee
hookLine: the Trustee, to whom affairs are entrusted
tomorrow: a man with nothing reaches a crowded well. what does he do?

lines: WHAT DO YOU DO WITH THE WAIT?
cards: Results in two weeks, the email said. Amira has refreshed her inbox four times since breakfast, and checked the scholarship's website twice, as if it might update itself. The essay is in.
The interview is done. Last night she went back downstairs and told her dad the truth: it was medium. He laughed and said medium is fine.
Nothing left to do now but wait, and waiting has a weight all its own. So what do you do with it?

teach.b: Today's Name is for exactly this: Al-Wakil, the Trustee, the one to whom affairs are handed. Surah At-Talaq: "And whosoever putteth his trust in Allah, He will suffice him." But trust here isn't sitting on your hands.

A man once asked the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, whether he should tie up his camel and trust, or leave it loose and trust. The answer, in Jami' at-Tirmidhi: tie it, and trust. Amira tied every rope she had.
Now the camel is in other hands. Trust here isn't instead of the work. It's what comes after it.
Look back over the week and you'll see the ropes. Al-Hakim, wise: a hole in a boat that turned out to be a rescue. Al-Wadud, loving: flashcards before sunrise.
Al-Majid, glorious: out loud or under your breath. Al-Ba'ith, he raises: tomatoes after rain. Ash-Shahid, witnessed: an ID under a chair.
Al-Haqq, the truth: medium, not great. Here's the line to tell a friend tonight.
In Surah Al Imran, people warned of a great force gathered against them answered: hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil, Allah is enough for us, and the best Trustee.
Two weeks of Names in one breath: Al-Hasib, who is enough, and Al-Wakil, who holds what you've handed over.

how: Muslims say hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil (3:173) in hard moments, and the hadith 'tie it, and trust' (Jami' at-Tirmidhi) is taught to show that trust in Allah comes after doing one's part.

o: the guardian who writes every rule
the Trustee, who takes what you hand over
the one who keeps a record of all debts

games.q: two weeks of Names — tap the pairs.
p: a dead land revived by rain

s: trusting Allah means leaving the camel untied
hasbunallahu wa ni'mal wakil joins Al-Wakil with 'Allah is enough for us'
3:173: Allah is enough for us, and the best Trustee.
Khidr holed the boat to protect its owners
a king was seizing every sound boat (Al-Hakim's day).

games.q: your sister's job interview went well, and now she can't sleep for checking her email. what fits Al-Wakil?
o: 'you tied the camel. hand the result over, and check once a day.'
'trusting God means you should stop hoping for the job.'
'keep refreshing; trust means watching closely for the answer.'
games.why: tie it, and trust: do your part, then hand the rest to al-Wakil. trust doesn't cancel hope, and it doesn't need a refresh button.

practice: Rest your hands in your lap, palms up. Name one worry, quietly, and let it sit in your open hands, with its weight. Then tip your hands, just slightly, as if passing it to someone you trust.
Notice whether your hands feel any different. Leave them open for the sit.

wordCard.voice: Al-Wakil. The Trustee, the one you hand your affairs to, once the camel is tied. Name fifty-two, and two weeks of Names are done.

orig.note: Arabic: the Trustee, the one affairs are handed to. 3:173: ni'mal wakil, the best Trustee.

carryVoice: The two weeks' last line: entrusted, the camel tied and the rope let go. Until next week.

sources.q: And whosoever putteth his trust in Allah, He will suffice him.

sources.ref: Jami' at-Tirmidhi 3507 (the list of the Names, including al-Wakil)
